title: Ultrasonic Testing for Power Plants | UT Inspection (US)
description: Ultrasonic thickness and weld inspection for US fossil, combined cycle and hydro plants: boilers, HRSGs, B31.1 piping and FAC programs. Request a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Power Plants: UT Thickness and Weld Inspection in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing (UT) on boilers, heat recovery steam generators, B31.1 steam and feedwater piping, and hydro penstocks at power plants across the United States. The work is mostly wall-thickness surveys for flow-accelerated corrosion and shear wave examination of welds during planned outages. Technicians are mobilized to your plant for the agreed scope and the data goes to your inspector or engineer. Request a UT inspection quote with the component list and outage dates.

What ultrasonic testing is used for in a power plant

A generating station is a pressure-retaining system that runs hot, cycles often, and loses metal in predictable places. Ultrasonic testing answers two questions that dominate outage planning: how much wall is left, and is there a planar flaw in a weld that surface methods cannot see. Thickness work covers feedwater lines, economizer outlets, cold reheat and hot reheat piping, extraction steam, drain lines, deaerator shells, condensate piping and the tight-radius elbows where flow changes direction. Weld work covers circumferential and longitudinal seams on headers, drums, steam piping and attachments that were repaired or replaced during the outage.

UT is a volumetric method, so it reaches the middle of a wall that magnetic particle and penetrant testing never touch. It is also single-sided: a technician can often examine a pipe weld from the outside with the line in place, without removing insulation more than a few inches beyond the weld. The tradeoff is surface condition and geometry. Heavy scale, pitted external surfaces and small-bore connections need preparation or a different method. Our national ultrasonic testing page describes the method in general; this page is about the equipment you actually have.

Boilers, HRSGs and heat recovery equipment

Utility and industrial boilers are built to ASME Section I, and the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC) governs repairs and alterations after they enter service. State boiler inspectors and authorized inspection agencies decide what must be examined and when; Atlantis supplies the measurements and the reports they review. In a conventional boiler the thickness targets are the waterwall tubes at burner levels, superheater and reheater bends, economizer tubes where ash erodes the outside, and drum and header nozzle welds. For a single tube the tube-specific work is on a separate page: ultrasonic boiler tube inspection.

Combined cycle plants add heat recovery steam generators, where feedwater and low-pressure evaporator circuits lose wall to flow-accelerated corrosion, and where cycling produces thermal fatigue at tube-to-header joints and attemperator stations. A typical HRSG scope pairs a thickness grid on the low-pressure drum downcomers and economizer headers with shear wave examination of repaired nozzle and attachment welds. Duct burner supports and casing penetrations are often added when the unit has been cycled hard. Access is the real constraint: HRSG modules are tall and tight, and scaffold, lift or rope access is arranged by the plant under its own permits.

Flow-accelerated corrosion and thickness monitoring

Flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) is the main reason power plants run ultrasonic thickness programs. Single-phase and two-phase flow strips the protective oxide from carbon steel, thinning it quietly from the inside until a pipe ruptures. Industry guidance from EPRI and the plant's own FAC program identify susceptible lines, rank them, and set the grid locations. Atlantis technicians take the readings at the locations in your program, mark the grid on the pipe so the next outage repeats the same points, and report raw readings alongside the minimum found. We do not rank components, predict wear rate or calculate remaining life; your FAC engineer does that from our data.

Repeatability matters more than anything else in this work. A reading that moves by a few thousandths between outages may be real wear or may be a different transducer position. We therefore record grid origin and orientation on a sketch, note the surface temperature, and use the same calibration block material and transducer type each visit. Where the same grid is read year after year, a consistent technique is worth more than a more elaborate one. Our guide to ASME Section V Article 5 thickness measurement requirements explains the calibration side in detail.

Piping under B31.1 and where UT fits

Power piping is designed and fabricated to ASME B31.1. The code sets design thickness and weld examination requirements; owners add in-service programs on top. For a plant that wants a full line survey, the ultrasonic pipe thickness testing page covers how we lay out condition monitoring locations, and our piping circuit inspection and CML page shows how the results are organized by circuit. Both apply to B31.1 systems as readily as to process piping. The same technician usually reads thickness and examines the adjacent weld in one visit, which keeps insulation removal and scaffold time to a minimum.

Welds in steam piping are examined by angle beam techniques against the acceptance criteria of the governing code, the repair procedure or the owner's specification. When a weld is new or repaired, the procedure and acceptance criteria usually come from the construction code or repair plan; for in-service examination the owner or authorized inspector states the criteria. We state in the report which document was used. See the guide to ASME Section V Article 4 ultrasonic examination for how procedures are structured.

Turbines, generators and hydro assets

Rotating equipment and hydro structures call for different judgment. On steam turbines and generators, UT is applied to components made from forgings and castings: casing flanges, rotor and shaft sections, and attachment bolting, where the owner or turbine service provider supplies the acceptance criteria. Those parts are covered in ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings. On hydro projects, penstock shell plate and the girth and longitudinal welds are examined for laminations, thinning and weld flaws, usually in conjunction with the owner's dam safety engineer. Penstocks are confined, wet and steep, so the owner arranges ventilation, rescue and fall protection.

Nuclear balance-of-plant work, such as secondary-side piping and non-safety-related components, is accepted only where the owner's program permits it. Atlantis does not hold 10 CFR 50 Appendix B or NQA-1 qualification and does not work on safety-related components that require it.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT on power equipment

Ultrasonic testing finds wall loss and internal weld flaws. When the concern is a surface crack at a weld toe, a fillet or an attachment, magnetic particle inspection for power plants is the faster and more sensitive tool on ferritic steel. On austenitic stainless, nickel alloys and nonferrous parts, liquid penetrant testing for power plants is the alternative because magnetic methods do not work. Many outage scopes use all three: UT for thickness and volumetric flaws, MT or PT to confirm surface condition after grinding out a defect. Telling us which weld is being repaired, and why, lets us propose the right combination.

Method choice for common power plant components
ComponentConcernMethod
Feedwater and extraction pipingFlow-accelerated wall lossUT thickness grid
Header and drum nozzle weldsFatigue cracking, lack of fusionUT shear wave, then MT on the surface
Stainless steam linesSurface cracksPT
Penstock plateThinning, laminationsUT thickness and straight beam
Turbine casing flangesCracks after repairMT or PT per owner criteria

How we examine: calibration, couplant and temperature

Technique details separate a useful power plant report from a table of numbers. Thickness gauges are calibrated on blocks of the same acoustic velocity as the pipe, with a two-point check before and after each shift. High-temperature piping calls for a high-temperature couplant and a transducer rated for the surface; where the surface is above the safe contact range, the line is measured when it is cooled or the reading is corrected for temperature. Surface preparation is by wire brush or flapper wheel to bright metal; paint thickness is measured and subtracted only when the gauge is set up for it.

Weld examination uses shear wave transducers of the angle and frequency set in the procedure, with distance amplitude correction or a reference reflector at the required sensitivity. Scan coverage is documented on a sketch. Crew members hold qualifications issued under Atlantis's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the scan and calls the indications, while an ASNT Level III signs off the procedure and checks the finished report. Our quality system carries ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates.

What the report contains

  • Plant, unit, system and component identifiers matching your drawings or isometrics
  • Procedure number, revision and the code or specification used for acceptance
  • Instrument, transducer, couplant and calibration block, with calibration checks
  • Technician name and qualification level
  • Thickness grids or CML readings, with minimum, nominal and sketch of grid origin
  • Weld indications with location, length, amplitude and accept or reject against the named criteria
  • Surface temperature, condition and any limits on coverage

Reports go to the named contact in a format your inspection database can import. Atlantis does not decide fitness for service, set the next inspection date or sign as the authorized inspector.

What to send for a quote

  • Unit list, drawings, isometrics or FAC grid sheets
  • Material, nominal and minimum thickness, and operating temperature range
  • Code or specification, including B31.1, Section I, NBIC or an owner standard
  • Quantity of grid points or welds, and whether welds are new, repaired or in service
  • Insulation, scaffold and access plan, confined space status and permits
  • Outage window, site badging or background check requirements and the site address

Planning an outage scope

Outage work is scheduled by the plant, and thickness crews are often the first on the line because their findings feed repair decisions. Plants usually give technicians site orientation, lockout and tagout training, and, at some stations, fitness-for-duty or background screening. We mobilize technicians who are prepared for those requirements and ask for them early in the quoting process. Insulation removal, scaffold and any rope or lift access are arranged by the site, not by us. Because findings can change the outage scope, plants often hold a short review each day; Atlantis technicians report indications to the plant's inspector as they are found rather than at the end of the job.

What we do not do on power projects

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 or Agreement State rules. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page, we do not calculate remaining life or fitness for service, and we do not act as the authorized inspector. We provide ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant data that those people rely on.

Where we work in the US for power generation

Atlantis technicians travel to your site from wherever the work is. These city pages describe power-generation context in each region:

  • Charlotte: the Carolinas coal-to-gas conversions and combined cycle additions that keep FAC programs active.
  • Knoxville: the Tennessee Valley, with fossil and hydro units under one regional grid.
  • Atlanta: Southeastern combined cycle stations and the load-following duty that wears HRSGs.
  • Birmingham: Alabama steam plants, with a long fabrication history behind them.
  • Phoenix: Southwestern peaking and combined cycle plants working through high summer loads.
  • Chicago: Midwestern steam and district energy plants with older piping.
  • Pittsburgh: Ohio River Valley generating stations and heavy forging suppliers.
  • Tampa: Florida gas-fired units where humidity affects external corrosion.

Training your own technicians

Some plants prefer to build in-house capability for routine thickness checks. Our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training teach the method, and the power generation NDT training page describes what applies to plants. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its technicians; we provide the course content and practice, and a written practice can be set up for your site. The ultrasonic simulator lets trainees practice before they handle real equipment.

faq.q: What does UT find on a power plant boiler or HRSG?
faq.a: Ultrasonic testing measures remaining wall on tubes, headers, drums and piping, and finds internal flaws in welds such as lack of fusion and cracks. It does not find tiny surface cracks reliably, so magnetic particle or penetrant testing is added after grinding or on suspect welds.

faq.q: Can you do thickness readings on a line that is still hot?
faq.a: Yes, within limits. We use high-temperature couplant and a transducer rated for the surface, and the procedure states the maximum temperature. If the line is too hot to touch safely, the reading is taken after it cools or at a lower-temperature location agreed with your inspector.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication or a thickness reading is acceptable?
faq.a: Acceptance comes from the governing code, repair plan or owner specification named in the report. Atlantis reports against the criteria you supply. Remaining life, repair or replacement decisions, and the next inspection date belong to your engineer or authorized inspector.

faq.q: Do you support flow-accelerated corrosion programs?
faq.a: We take thickness readings at the grid locations your FAC program specifies, mark and sketch the grid for repeat visits, and deliver raw data and minimums. We do not rank susceptible lines or predict wear rates; that analysis stays with your FAC engineer.

faq.q: Can you work under ASME B31.1 and Section I?
faq.a: Yes. We examine piping and boiler components against the criteria in B31.1, ASME Section I, NBIC repair documents or your own specification, using a procedure approved by an ASNT Level III. The report names the document used for every acceptance decision.

faq.q: Do you work on nuclear plants?
faq.a: Only on balance-of-plant, non-safety-related scope where the owner allows it. Atlantis does not hold 10 CFR 50 Appendix B or NQA-1 qualification, so safety-related components are outside our scope.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a plant outage?
faq.a: Send the unit and system list, drawings or grid sheets, material and thickness, operating temperature, governing code, quantity of points or welds, and outage dates. Also tell us about access, insulation, badging, background checks and permits so we can plan technicians correctly.

Qualification comes through the Atlantis written practice, which is built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II runs the scan and interprets what it shows, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates cover the company.

faq.q: When is magnetic particle or penetrant testing the better choice at a power plant?
faq.a: Use MT on ferritic steel when a surface crack at a weld toe or fillet is the concern, and PT on stainless, nickel alloy or nonferrous parts. UT is the choice when wall loss or an internal flaw is the question.
